playbook:
When the escort stage comes up every round, I always name a boat — never "none." A mutual escort pays 5 points, dwarfing anything else in the game, and naming none guarantees zero. Default to naming the same live boat every round and use my station note to signal that I'm escorting them, to get them to reciprocate.

When I post a note, I use it to coordinate escorts explicitly: "Echo escorts Foxtrot this round — Foxtrot name me back." Notes are my only coordination channel and the biggest scoring lever, so I never waste them on flavor like "steady on station."

When the claim stage comes up, I always report truthfully — the rules say the claim must match my private result, and false claims risk detection and burned trust I need for escort coordination.

When I fire, I follow the standing order (my assigned next station) unless the points math says otherwise. I only fire on Harbor if I'm far behind late in the game — 3 points transferred sounds good but Harbor's jettison threat means retaliation and lost board time; early on it's never worth it.

When I choose a fire cell, I track the target's past hide cells from the public round logs and fire at the cell they favor most. If no pattern exists, I fire at central cells (4–6), which arbitrary and biased hiders both hit more often.

When I hide, I avoid my previous hide cells and any repeated number — in my past play I got hit repeatedly because I was readable. I rotate among extremes (1, 2, 8, 9) and vary round to round, since opponents likely follow the same central-cell logic I do.

When I've been hit multiple rounds by the same opponent, I note it publicly ("Gamma has hit Echo three rounds running") — it may discourage them or at least costs nothing since notes are free.

When it's the final rounds and escort pairs haven't formed, I double down on one partner and explicitly bargain in my note ("I'll name you every round if you name me") rather than giving up with "none."

Standing rule: escort claims first, honest claim reports, ordered fire at pattern-predicted cells, unpredictable hides, notes spent only on coordination.

1.text:
- When the scoreboard shows me behind, I stop both-sides-loss exchanges and look for a better source of points — shooting only earns me 4 but my cycle opponent earns the same off me, so pure gunnery politics never closes a gap; escort pairs (5 each) do.
- When I choose an escort claim, I always name a boat and never "none" — mutual escort is the biggest point source in the game and "none" can never score. I use my station note each round to propose a specific pairing ("Foxtrot names Gamma — Gamma name me back") with one boat, consistently, until one reciprocates.
- When a rival publicly proposes mutual escort, I name them back immediately and keep doing it every round they reciprocate.
- When I pick a hide cell, I ignore opponents' notes like "I'm at 7" — notes commit to nothing. I track only observed behavior: which cells my designated shooter has actually fired, and I hide away from those, not in them. I vary my hide every round within a small set of cells my shooter has never hit, since repeating a cell that got me hit is how I bled points.
- When I fire, I treat target choice as fixed by standing order — I always fire at my assigned station, never at Harbor (its retaliation threat plus jettison rules make the 3-point grab a trap, and I lose standing with whoever survives to shoot me later). I spend my reasoning on the cell, not the target.
- When I pick a fire cell, I shoot where my target last hid or the cell before it in their rotation — hiders repeat more than they should, myself included. I don't waste shots on extreme cells (1, 9) unless I've seen the target use them.
- When I file a hit/miss claim, I always report the office's result truthfully — the claim must match the private result, so there is nothing to gain by deviating.
- When I post a note, I make it short, consistent, and transactional: one standing coordination offer (escort pairing, or a no-fire truce with the boat that shoots me in exchange for my escort), repeated verbatim each round so it's credible.
- When trailing late with a couple of rounds left, I send one explicit deal note to my shooter ("stop hitting me and I'll escort you every remaining round") — a mutual escort stream (5/round) beats the 4/−1 shooting exchange for both of us, which makes the deal rational for them.
- When scores are roughly level, I keep it simple: hide unpredictably, fire at my target's most likely cell, claim truthfully, and push one escort pairing until it lands.

2.text:
When the board is 9 cells and I have no information, I hide near the edges (1–2, 8–9), not the salient center, and I fire close to the center (4–6) because unsophisticated opponents tend to hide there — I wasted six rounds firing cell 9 and never hit once from it.

When I fire, I vary the cell slightly round to round around my best estimate of the opponent's hiding habit, rather than repeating the exact same cell every round, so an opponent tracking my shots can't simply avoid that cell.

When choosing my hide, I look at who fires at me under the standing order and move off any cell I've repeated; I never hide in the cell the player targeting me just hit or narrowly missed if they've shown a pattern of aiming at one spot.

I always claim the true result the office gives me, since the claim must match it and attempting anything else is wasted; I don't spend reasoning effort on the claim stage at all.

I treat escort claims as the biggest source of free points: in the note stage I explicitly propose a mutual escort pact with one named boat ("I escort you, you escort me"), then I file that boat at the escort stage. Filing "none" every round leaves 5–10 points on the table, which can exceed what shooting earns.

I never fire at Harbor. Avoiding the +3 jettison bounty is not worth the risk of being put off the board entirely; I follow the standing-order target unless Harbor is somehow the only option, and even then I fire on the ordered station.

When coordinating escorts, I pick the boat least likely to score hits on me (the one whose standing order points elsewhere) so the pact doesn't conflict with survival, and I keep naming them consistently so they learn to reciprocate.

I keep my note short and consistent with my pact plan: use it as the coordination channel, since it's the only public broadcast I get each round.

If a pact partner stops reciprocating my escort, I drop them the next round and propose to the remaining boat rather than filing "none" again.

I track the scoreboard when hides and targets are chosen: if I'm ahead late, I prioritize hiding away from whoever is shooting at me over maximizing my own shot; if I'm behind, I concentrate fire on the most predictable hider, even off standing order only if the rule allows it without penalty.
